answers.answer: The client sends its request to the service entry point; the reverse-proxy balancer forwards it to a selected application backend, which performs the work and returns its response through the balancer to the client. Choose L7 to distinguish /search from /purchase and send them to different pools. It needs readable HTTP contents; for HTTPS the proxy normally terminates client TLS, with backend encryption configured separately. L4 typically selects a backend per TCP connection using network information, so many requests reusing that connection may all reach the same backend without a new selection. A single adequate server can suffice when neither traffic distribution nor redundant serving is needed.

evidence.quote: In a reverse-proxy arrangement, the client contacts one service entry point. The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend, which performs the operation and returns a response through the balancer to the client.
Routes at the transport level. For TCP traffic, it typically chooses a backend for a connection using network information, not HTTP paths.
Many HTTP requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.

Understands HTTP requests. It can route /images and /reports to different backend groups, or select a backend for each request. Rules that keep a user on one backend can override independent selection.

Path routing requires readable HTTP contents. TLS encrypts the connection; an HTTPS proxy normally ends, or terminates, that TLS connection to inspect requests. Encryption to the backend is a separate configuration choice.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving.

answers.answer: Round robin controls turns across eligible backends; it is simple for similar servers and work, but a cheap lookup and a long request each count as one, hiding their unequal cost. Least connections selects by active connection count and can help with varying durations, but connections can carry very different amounts of work. Weights control traffic share; twice the measured capacity suggests starting with twice the weight, but configured weights neither measure current load nor guarantee performance. Evaluate latency and resource use before choosing. Another API backend adds API capacity, which cannot remove the saturated shared database bottleneck. After failure, clients must have a reachable alternate entry path through an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working, tested failover; merely drawing another balancer is insufficient. Surviving backends need spare capacity sufficient for remaining traffic, or redistribution can overload them; visibly limit or reject excess work. Verify the whole path under representative traffic and a failure.

evidence.quote: Takes turns across eligible backends. It is a simple starting point for similar servers and similar work; a quick read and a slow report still each count as one request.
Prefers the backend with fewer active connections. This can help when connection durations vary, but one connection may carry far more work than another.
Bias the share of traffic. A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. Configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee.
For long, uneven work, consider least connections; for unequal server capacity, consider weights. Check actual latency and resource use before deciding: no policy is universally best.
Balancing distributes existing capacity. More API servers can help when API processing is the bottleneck; they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.

Headroom is spare capacity. After one backend fails, the survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load. Otherwise redirecting traffic can overload them. Limit or reject excess work visibly instead of assuming redistribution solves it.

A lone balancer is itself a possible failure point. If it fails, clients need a reachable alternate entry path, not just another disconnected balancer box. Use an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working failover, and test that path.
Measure request latency, errors and backend and database resource use under representative traffic, including a failure. Redundant components alone do not guarantee an available service.

answers.answer: A 200 health response only shows the probed endpoint answered; it does not establish that purchases can access their required database. A readiness check should reflect capabilities needed to serve useful application work, including that dependency here. Even this check samples limited capabilities at intervals and may use failure thresholds; the backend can fail immediately after a pass, so detection is delayed. Once detected and removed from eligibility it stops receiving new selections, subject to checking the product's all-unhealthy behavior. Existing requests may still fail: removal cannot complete, undo, or safely replay them.

evidence.quote: A health check periodically probes a backend. Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while an application handler cannot reach its required database.

Use a check that reflects the capabilities needed to serve application requests. Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.
Check the product's all-unhealthy policy too. Some balancers send traffic to unhealthy targets when every target fails its checks, rather than refusing all traffic.

answers.answer: B cannot read the cart held only in A's memory, and failure of A can lose the only copy. Sticky routing prefers A for that customer, keeping ordinary requests with the cart, but it can skew load and restrict placement. It neither copies the cart nor guarantees survival when A fails. Shared session storage lets A or B read the cart, at the cost of access or coordination work and another shared dependency whose availability matters. Consistent routing and state availability on another server are separate responsibilities.

evidence.quote: Session state is information kept between a user's requests. If a server keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.
Prefers the same backend for that user's requests. It can keep ordinary requests on A, but skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails.
Lets either backend read the session. It adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.
Routing a user consistently and making their state available on another server are separate responsibilities.

answers.answer: First stop new assignments to A, then allow its accepted 20-second request and other in-flight work to finish within a bounded deadline. Handle existing connection lifetimes or stop further HTTP requests on them, and track already accepted work; shut down after completion or deadline expiry. New assignments introduce additional work, whereas the accepted request is already underway and needs time to finish. Stopping new L4 connections alone leaves the reused connection able to carry more HTTP requests to A. Thus draining must account for whether selection occurs per connection or request: manage existing connections for L4 and track accepted requests for L7. Deadline expiry can force termination and interrupt unfinished work, which is not automatically transferred to B. The deadline duration is unspecified, so whether this particular 20-second request finishes before shutdown cannot be determined.

evidence.quote: During a deployment, draining stops new assignments to A while allowing in-flight work, meaning requests already underway, to finish within a deadline. Shut A down after completion or when that deadline expires.

Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.
Give a running request time to finish, but bound the wait. Forced termination at the deadline may interrupt unfinished requests. Their work is not automatically moved to B.

answers.answer: A lost response leaves the client unable to distinguish a completed purchase from one that did not complete, although the stated purchase did commit. A blind retry on B can therefore apply the purchase effect again. Use one stable idempotency key for this logical purchase on every attempt, and let all backends consult a shared durable key/result record. In one transaction uniquely reserve the key, apply the purchase effect, and record the result, committing all or none. A repeat then returns the recorded result without applying the effect again; separate check-then-write operations could race or leave a crash gap. A fresh retry key does not identify the same logical operation, while A-only memory does not reliably protect a retry handled elsewhere. Limit attempts and delay retries because extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload. Retry policy alone supplies neither duplicate protection nor guaranteed success.

evidence.quote: A backend commits a write, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write completed. A blind retry on another backend can repeat the effect.

A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt. Deduplication means recognizing a repeat. A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in one server's memory, cannot reliably protect retries elsewhere.

All backends use a shared durable record of the key and result. In one database transaction, reserve the key uniquely, apply the effect and record the result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without applying the effect again. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
Bound retry attempts and delay them: extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload. Retry policy does not replace duplicate protection or guarantee success.
